687.title: The Dedication of the Lateran (9 November)
687.hook: the pope's own cathedral, mother of all churches
687.howItsDone: Catholics everywhere keep the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica on 9 November, the cathedral of the bishop of Rome; when it falls on a Sunday it replaces the Sunday in Ordinary Time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Souls, candles on the graves and names read aloud. Your line was we remember.

Quick question: what's the pope's cathedral? Most people say Saint Peter's: it's the biggest, it's where the pope says the big Masses, it's on every postcard. But it's the wrong answer. The pope is the bishop of Rome, and the bishop of Rome's cathedral is across the city, in a quieter neighborhood near the old walls: the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran. Carved on its front, in Latin, is a claim no other church makes. And on the ninth of November, every Catholic parish in the world keeps the birthday of this one building.
screen: `NOT SAINT PETER'S.` → `THE BISHOP OF ROME'S CATHEDRAL.` → `A BIRTHDAY FOR A BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The land once belonged to a Roman family, the Laterani, and then to the emperor. After Constantine made Christianity legal, he gave the property to the bishop of Rome, and a basilica was built and dedicated in the early 300s, traditionally by Pope Sylvester. It was the first great public church in the city. For roughly a thousand years the popes lived next door, in the Lateran Palace, until they moved to Avignon in the 1300s, and five ecumenical councils met there. The full name is the Archbasilica of the Most Holy Savior and of Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist. The inscription on the front calls it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world. That's why the feast is kept everywhere. It isn't about Roman architecture; it's about belonging. Every parish, in Lagos or Lima or Little Rock, is connected to this one, through its bishop, to the bishop of Rome. The feast ranks high enough that when the ninth of November falls on a Sunday, it replaces the ordinary Sunday. The Gospel for the day is Jesus driving the sellers out of the Temple, and the second reading is Paul's question to Corinth, in the Douay-Rheims: "Know you not, that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" The feast does what that line does. It honors a building, then turns around and says: the real building is the people.

Then picture the people: the usher, the choir, the family that's always late, the old man in the back pew. If you pray, pray for that church and those people by name; if you don't belong to a parish, picture any community you belong to.

688.title: Christ the King
688.hook: the year's last Sunday, instituted in 1925
688.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, on the last Sunday of the liturgical year, the Sunday before Advent; some parishes hold a Eucharistic procession or a holy hour.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dedication of the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral. Your line was the mother church.

Crowns had fallen all over Europe in the First World War, and new movements were promising that the nation, or the party, or the leader, deserved everything. Into that, in December 1925, Pope Pius XI published a letter announcing a brand-new feast. Its name sounded old-fashioned even then: Christ the King. Real kings were losing their thrones, and the Church named a king who never sat on one. Today it's the last Sunday of the Church's year, the week before Advent starts again.
screen: `1925: KINGS FALLEN, NEW POWERS RISING.` → `A NEW FEAST.` → `THE YEAR'S LAST SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: Pius XI's letter, Quas Primas, argued that many of the world's troubles came from pushing Christ out of public life, and that people needed reminding whose kingdom outlasts all the others. At first the feast fell on the last Sunday of October. After the Second Vatican Council it moved to the last Sunday of the liturgical year, so the year now ends looking toward the end of all things. But here's the twist the feast is built on. Which king? Watch where the title lands in the passion. Before Pilate, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." The soldiers dress him in purple and crown him with thorns as a joke. And the sign nailed above his head, in three languages, says: "THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS." Rome meant it as mockery, a warning to anyone who claimed a crown. Christians came to read it as the plain truth. In one year of the cycle, the Gospel for this feast is that exact scene: Jesus on the cross, the sign above him, and a criminal beside him asking, Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom. In another, it's the sheep and the goats: the king who says, whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me. So the crown is thorns, the throne is a cross, and the king is found in the hungry and the prisoner. Catholics call him king, and then look at how he reigns.

689.title: The months have themes
689.hook: January the Holy Name, March Joseph, May Mary, June the Sacred Heart, October the rosary, November the dead
689.howItsDone: Many Catholics follow traditional monthly devotions, such as May for Mary with May crownings, June for the Sacred Heart, October for the rosary and November for the dead; these are popular customs, not part of the official liturgical calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ the King, crowned with thorns. Your line was king on a cross.

In some Catholic homes, May means fresh flowers in front of a statue of Mary, and November means a list of the family's dead tucked beside the candles. Under the feasts walked all year, from Advent to Christ the King, there's a second, quieter calendar. Not days. Months. Each month has its own devotion, and where families keep them, they shape what's on the shelf and what's prayed at night.
screen: `MAY FLOWERS, NOVEMBER NAMES.` → `A SECOND, QUIETER CALENDAR.` → `MONTHS, NOT DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, what this isn't. The month themes aren't part of the official liturgical calendar. No rule requires them; the Mass doesn't change because it's May. They're popular devotions, encouraged by popes, and customs vary from country to country. Here's the common pattern. January, the Holy Name of Jesus, the name given at his circumcision on the eighth day after Christmas. March, Saint Joseph, whose feast falls on the nineteenth. May, Mary: flowers before her statue, and in some parishes a May crowning, where a child sets a wreath on Mary's head. June, the Sacred Heart, since its feast usually falls then. July, often the Precious Blood. October, the rosary, the month of the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary on the seventh. November, the holy souls, the dead, opening with All Saints and All Souls. Look at what the months are doing. They follow the feasts, and stretch a single day into a season of attention. And they map onto ordinary life: Mary in spring flowers, the dead as the leaves come down in the north. A line from Ecclesiastes, in the Douay-Rheims, fits the whole idea: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." A month is long enough to form a habit. The feast is the door; the month is the room behind it.

690.title: Every Friday
690.hook: every Friday is a small day of penance, meat or another sacrifice by local rule
690.howItsDone: Catholic canon law makes every Friday a day of penance; many Catholics abstain from meat on all Fridays, and where bishops permit, as in the United States outside Lent, others choose a different penance such as charity or prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the months and their themes, like the May crowning. Your line was every month a door.

Why does a fast-food chain famous for burgers sell a fish sandwich? The story told in the business world is that a franchise owner in a Catholic neighborhood was losing money every Friday because his customers wouldn't eat meat that day. So he came up with a fish sandwich, and it went national. Whatever the details, the custom behind the story is real: Catholics going without meat on Fridays. And the reason sits under every week of the year, not just Lent.
screen: `A FISH SANDWICH FOR FRIDAYS.` → `NO MEAT ON FRIDAYS.` → `A REASON UNDER EVERY WEEK.`

segments.voice: The word is abstinence, from the Latin abstinere, to hold back. In Church law it means one thing: not eating meat. Fasting is different; it means eating less, one full meal. Catholics fast and abstain on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain on the Fridays of Lent. But canon law goes further. Every Friday of the year is a day of penance, kept in memory of the day Jesus died: a small Good Friday. The law names abstinence from meat as the usual way to keep it, from age fourteen, unless a solemnity falls on that Friday, and it lets each country's bishops set the details. That's where it gets local. In the United States since 1966, outside of Lent, the bishops allow Catholics to choose another penance instead: an act of charity, extra prayer, giving up something else. In England and Wales, the bishops brought back the meat rule in 2011. So a Catholic in London and one in Chicago may keep Friday differently, and both are keeping the law. Why meat and not, say, bread? One common explanation is that meat was the feast-day food, the one people looked forward to. Either way, the point was never that meat is bad. It's a small, regular no that makes room for a larger yes. Jesus put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily."

Keep it small enough to keep. If you pray, offer it for someone; if you don't, notice how holding back feels.

691.title: Ember and Rogation days
691.hook: old seasonal fasting days to bless the harvest and the fields
691.howItsDone: Since 1969, Ember and Rogation days are set by each bishops' conference and are little kept in many places; some parishes, especially rural ones, still hold Rogation processions to bless fields and gardens in spring, and some Catholics keep the Ember days as voluntary days of fasting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every Friday and the word abstinence. Your line was every friday a little lent.

In English villages, there was once a spring day when the whole parish went for a walk. The priest led the way with a cross, the choir sang, and the people followed the edge of the parish, field by field, stopping at boundary stones and old trees to pray for the crops. Children were sometimes bumped against the markers so they'd remember where the line was. It was called beating the bounds, and it belonged with a set of old fasting and praying days that are easy to miss on today's calendar.
screen: `A WHOLE PARISH ON A WALK.` → `PRAYING FIELD BY FIELD.` → `TWO OLDER PIECES.`

segments.voice: First, the Ember days. Four times a year, near the turn of each season, the Church kept three days of fasting and prayer: a Wednesday, a Friday and a Saturday. Their Latin name was quattuor tempora, the four times: in Advent, in Lent, after Pentecost, and in September after the feast of the Holy Cross. They were very old, and some historians think they grew from Rome's own seasons of harvest, vintage and sowing. They gave thanks for each season and asked a blessing on the next, and Ember Saturdays became the traditional days for ordinations. Then the Rogation days, from the Latin rogare, to ask. Tradition says that around 470, in Vienne in Gaul, after fires, earthquakes and wild animals had terrified the town, Bishop Mamertus called three days of fasting and processions before Ascension Thursday. The custom spread, and Rogation processions through the fields, asking God to bless the planting, became part of village life in many lands. Since the calendar reform of 1969, both are left to each country's bishops, and where they aren't kept, they've faded. But the instinct behind them is as old as the Psalms. As one psalm puts it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The earth hath yielded her fruit." Food doesn't start in the store. It starts in soil, weather and somebody's work, and these days were the Church remembering that out loud.

segments.voice: Pick up something you'll eat today, an apple, a slice of bread, a handful of rice, or picture your last meal, and trace it backward: the store, the truck, the warehouse, the farm, the field, the rain, the hands that picked it. Stay with each step for a breath. If you pray, ask God to bless the fields and the people who work them; if you don't, simply be grateful, step by step.

692.title: Saturday for Mary
692.hook: many Catholics give Saturdays to Mary
692.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary or a Marian prayer on Saturdays; on free Saturdays in Ordinary Time a parish may celebrate the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday, and some keep the Fatima devotion of the five first Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ember and Rogation days, quattuor tempora, old fasts that asked God to bless the harvest. Your line was bless the fields.

Ask an older Catholic what Friday is for, and you may hear about fish. For centuries Friday was a day without meat, kept in memory of the cross, and Catholics are still asked to mark it with some small penance. Sunday belongs to the resurrection. That leaves the day in between, the one that so often goes to laundry and errands. In many Catholic homes and parishes, by an old and quiet custom, Saturday belongs to Mary.
screen: `FRIDAY: THE CROSS.` → `SUNDAY: THE RESURRECTION.` → `SATURDAY: AN OLD, QUIET CUSTOM.`

segments.voice: Nobody can point to the day this began. The custom grew slowly in the monasteries of the early Middle Ages. Alcuin of York, a scholar at Charlemagne's court around the year 800, is often credited with writing votive Masses for each day of the week, and he gave Saturday to Mary. Within a few centuries the Saturday Mass of Our Lady was common across Europe. Why Saturday? The sources don't settle it, but one answer has stuck. Think of Holy Saturday. Jesus lies in the tomb; the disciples have scattered and gone into hiding; the Gospels say almost nothing about that day. Tradition pictures Mary as the one who kept faith while everything was silent, waiting for Sunday. So every Saturday, the eve of every Sunday, is a small echo of that waiting. Luke gives her a habit that fits. After the shepherds leave Bethlehem, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Kept and pondered: a Saturday kind of faith. The custom is still in the Roman calendar. On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when no other memorial falls, a parish may keep the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday. In 1925 Sister Lúcia, one of the three Fatima children, said Mary had asked for a devotion of five first Saturdays: confession, Communion, the rosary and fifteen minutes of meditation. Many parishes still keep it. At home, the simplest way is the rosary, or even one decade of it. It's a custom, not a law, and not every Catholic keeps it. But it gives the week a shape: the cross, the waiting, the morning.
screen: `ALCUIN GIVES SATURDAY TO MARY.` · `HOLY SATURDAY: SHE KEPT FAITH.` · `A MEMORIAL STILL IN THE CALENDAR.` · `FIVE FIRST SATURDAYS.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS, PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: If you pray the rosary, take one decade slowly: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be, and let your fingers keep count so your mind doesn't have to. If you don't pray, or don't have beads, take ten slow breaths, and with each one bring back one thing from this week you'd like to keep and ponder, the way Luke says Mary did.

693.title: The Lord's Day
693.hook: every Sunday is a little Easter
693.howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday (or on Saturday evening) and to keep the day free of work that hinders worship, rest and time with family; many families also keep a shared Sunday meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saturday for Mary and the votive Mass. Your line was saturday is hers.

It's very early. A few women are walking out of Jerusalem carrying spices, worried about one practical thing: who will roll the stone away from the tomb? The Sabbath is over. It's the first day of the week, and the sun is coming up. When they get there, Mark says, the stone is already rolled back, and the tomb is empty. Out of that one morning, Christians built a habit that comes round every week.
screen: `VERY EARLY, CARRYING SPICES.` → `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `A WEEKLY HABIT.`

segments.voice: Each of the four Gospels puts the empty tomb early on the first day of the week, so the first day became the Christians' day. In Acts, the disciples at Troas, with Paul visiting, gather on the first day of the week to break bread. And the last book of the Bible gives the day its name. John, on the island of Patmos, writes in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." In the Latin of the Church, Sunday is still Dominica, the Lord's. Justin Martyr, writing to the Roman emperor, described the day called Sunday: Christians gathered from town and country, heard the writings of the apostles and prophets, prayed, and shared bread and wine, and a collection went to widows and orphans. Catholics reading it today recognize the Mass. Catholics speak of every Sunday as a little Easter: not a reminder of Easter, they say, but the same feast, coming round every seven days. The Second Vatican Council called Sunday the original feast day, the foundation of the whole year. Some early writers called it the eighth day: the old week ended with the Sabbath, the seventh, and they saw the resurrection as the first day of a new creation, outside the old count. Catholics keep it two ways: Mass, which the Church asks of them as an obligation, and rest, setting aside work that gets in the way of worship, joy and family. Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on it in 1998, Dies Domini, the day of the Lord. And week ninety-nine ends here: the Lateran, Christ the King, the months with their themes, then Friday, the Ember days, Mary's Saturday, and now Sunday, the day the whole week leans toward.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` · `I WAS IN THE SPIRIT ON THE LORD'S DAY.` · `JUSTIN DESCRIBES SUNDAY.` · `THE EIGHTH DAY: A NEW CREATION.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EASTER, EVERY SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Picture next Sunday from morning to night, with its noise, its errands, its inbox. Choose one thing to set down that day, a chore that can wait, a screen, a worry for Monday, and one thing to put in its place: a long meal, a walk, a call to someone you love, Mass if you go.
